design.summary: I read salvage/stream_vforce.json and verified its nine anchors against the live tree (all still count exactly 1) and its mechanism claims with grep/sed (all confirmed: `manual` is the right flag and `nuke` is raised nowhere; generations.js:902 floors every heavybomber pool at 6; DOMAIN at generations.js:397 includes gbr and fra; AIRFRAMES has zero gbr and zero fra rows, so both would fly as B-52s; unitFor at rules.js:4259 returns one airframe per faction/role/era and unitsFor has no callers; heavyair.js loads between eras.js and generations.js). The Blue Steel fatal is real and is fixed: Blue Steel entered RAF service February 1963 on Vulcan B.2s of 617, 27 and 83 Sqn and Victor B.2s of 100 and 139 and served to 1970, so it is now a modelled weapon (`bluesteel`, 9.6 tiles, the SAME Red Snow warhead and therefore the same dmg/aoe as Yellow Sun Mk.2 — the delivery changed, the warhead did not), and what was cancelled is named correctly as Blue Streak (1960), Blue Steel Mk.2 (Dec 1959) and Skybolt (22 Dec 1962). I found eleven further errors, two of them mechanical: the design's ASMP justification is arithmetically backwards (10.4 < 10.6, and entities.js:2150 holds a missile shot at range*0.88 so it really fired from 9.15), and its release gate is decorative for the AI because ai.js pickAirTarget falls into the harvester branch for role heavybomber. I deliver 14 edits — the V-force (Valiant e50, Vulcan e60 with Blue Steel plus Yellow Sun, Vulcan e80 Black Buck), the Mirage IV (IVA e60 with AN-11/AN-22, IVP e80–e90 with ASMP), five AIRFRAMES silhouettes, five stale comments corrected, and three small mechanism fixes without which the new rows either fire without permission or cannot fire at all. Britain gets nothing at e90/e00/e20 and France nothing at e50/e00/e20, each absence argued from a named date. All 14 applied cleanly to scratch copies with no brace imbalance and no double comma.

findings.what: The salvage design writes Blue Steel off as a non-capability, listing it beside two genuinely cancelled programmes, and builds the whole British thesis on that error ('Britain never fielded a stand-off round that worked', 'ASMP is the weapon Britain wanted and was refused', all three British rounds flat at 2.2 tiles). Blue Steel was in RAF service Feb 1963 - Vulcan B.2s of 617, 27, 83 Sqn and Victor B.2s of 100, 139 - launched at ~185 km at Mach 2.3 with the 1.1 Mt Red Snow warhead, and was the RAF's primary strategic weapon until the Polaris handover on 30 June 1969. Skybolt (22 Dec 1962) and Blue Streak (1960) are what was cancelled, and the Skybolt cancellation is why Blue Steel became the deterrent by default.

findings.what: Weapon release does not survive a tanker cycle, so a held-round aircraft that breaks off for fuel flies all the way back to the target and drops nothing. The carried-across strike literal omits `release`, and every hand-back assigns it straight to this.order rather than through setOrder(), the only place the token is stamped. Pre-exists for SEAD, but the Mirage IVA at radius 46 with a 2.0-tile bomb is the aircraft most likely in the game to hit bingo before weapon release.

findings.what: gbr_e60_tanker is named 'Victor K.2' with service 1974 but covers e60 to e80. The K.2 did not enter service until May 1974; the e60 tanker was the K.1, converted from 1965 precisely because the Valiant tankers had been grounded that January. The salvage design did not introduce this but writes it into three files as the justification for leaving the Victor off the bomber rows.

The salvage risks section claims 'no AIRCRAFT in the roster has ever carried a held round before', contradicting its own diagnosis ('every ARM') and the tree. Six aircraft carry a manual round as their only weapon and the game has a dedicated airborne self-release path for them. It matters only because it made the risk look larger than it is while hiding the two real mechanical holes.

THE V-FORCE. Valiant, Vulcan, Victor - Britain's airborne deterrent from
   February 1955 until the Royal Navy took it to sea with Polaris on 30 June
   1969, a handover this game already carries on the submarine side as
   gbr_e60_ssbn, HMS Resolution. Three aeroplanes, three different endings, so
   three different rows rather than three copies of one:
     VALIANT, 138 Squadron at RAF Gaydon, February 1955 - the first of the
     three and the first into combat, bombing Egyptian airfields at Suez in
     October 1956. It dropped Britain's first air-burst atomic weapon, a Blue
     Danube, at Maralinga on 11 October 1956, and the first British thermo-
     nuclear device, Short Granite, over Malden Island on 15 May 1957. In 1962
     the fleet was taken off high-level strike and handed to SACEUR for LOW
     level, because surface-to-air missiles had made 50,000 feet untenable -
     and low-level flying is what fatigued the rear spar. Cracks were found in
     August 1964 and the whole fleet was grounded on 26 January 1965. So its
     row is `to: "e50"` and stops, and it was killed by the same change in the
     threat that the rest of this arc is about.
     VULCAN B.2 holds e60 AND e80, two rows for two different jobs - the same
     thing the Buff and the H-6 above already do, on a shorter arc. 1963: Blue
     Steel, a hundred miles of stand-off. 1982: twenty-one 1,000 lb bombs and
     an overflight of Port Stanley. That is the British arc, and it goes the
     WRONG WAY round - reach in the sixties, none in the eighties - which is
     the single most interesting thing about it.
     VICTOR gets NO bomber row, and that is an answer rather than a gap. Its
     bomber career, November 1957 to 31 December 1968, sits entirely inside two
     bands already held by an aircraft that arrived first and left later, and
     unitFor() returns exactly ONE airframe per faction, role and era. What the
     Victor is in this game is what it became: gbr_e60_tanker, the tanker fleet
     that refuelled Black Buck eleven aircraft deep.
   WHY BRITAIN STOPS IN 1969 and the B-52 does not. Blue Steel was real and is
   modelled - in RAF service from February 1963 on Vulcan B.2s of 617, 27 and
   83 Squadrons and Victor B.2s of 100 and 139, launched at about 185 km at
   Mach 2.3, the RAF's primary strategic weapon until the Polaris handover and
   withdrawn in 1970. What Britain never got was its SUCCESSOR. Blue Steel
   Mk.2 was cancelled in December 1959, Blue Streak in 1960, and the American
   Skybolt on 22 December 1962 at Nassau - and it is the Skybolt cancellation
   that made Blue Steel the deterrent by default and the submarine the only
   way forward. So the e80 Vulcan is back to 2.2 tiles and the e90, e00 and e20
   bands are EMPTY and stay empty: 44 Squadron, the last Vulcan bomber
   squadron, disbanded on 21 December 1982 and 50 Squadron's Vulcan K.2 tankers
   went on 31 March 1984.

   MIRAGE IV. The airborne leg of the force de frappe, and the one nation here
   that built the aeroplane, the warhead and the stand-off missile itself.
   Prototype 17 June 1959; EB 1/91 Gascogne at Mont-de-Marsan on 1 October
   1964; 62 production aircraft. It is not a strategic bomber in the B-52 sense
   and the figures say so: a Mach 2.2 two-seat delta the size of a large
   fighter with a combat radius near 1,240 km. The reach was bought separately
   - twelve Boeing C-135F ordered in 1962 and delivered from 1964, plus
   Mirage-on-Mirage buddy tanking - and it lives on fra_e60_tanker, not on the
   bomber.
   e50 EMPTY, and for a named reason rather than an absence: there was no
   French warhead until Gerboise Bleue at Reggane on 13 February 1960, and the
   jet bomber France did have in that decade, the Sud-Ouest Vautour IIB of
   1958, was a tactical aircraft with nothing strategic to carry.
   e00 and e20 EMPTY: the strike role left this aeroplane on 1 July 1996 and
   passed to the two-seat Mirage 2000N and later the Rafale B, which are
   fighter airframes carrying one missile and are on the French roster as
   fighters and strike aircraft, not as bombers. The last Mirage IVs flew
   strategic RECONNAISSANCE, not strike, until 23 June 2005.


   Loaded after eras.js so it can add to the roster and reindex.            */
edits.why: Documents both new families in the file's own voice and says which bands are EMPTY and why. Corrects the salvage fatal: Avro Blue Steel entered RAF service February 1963 on Vulcan B.2s (617, 27, 83 Sqn) and Victor B.2s (100, 139) and served to 1970; what was cancelled is Blue Streak (1960), Blue Steel Mk.2 (Dec 1959) and Skybolt (22 December 1962, Nassau), and the Skybolt cancellation is precisely what made Blue Steel the deterrent by default. Also corrects Operation Grapple - Short Granite fell over Malden Island on 15 May 1957, not Christmas Island, which was the staging base. Anchor verified count 1 and repeated at the foot.

edits.why: Adds the rounds these aircraft actually carried, including the one the salvage design wrongly wrote off. Blue Steel shares the Red Snow warhead with Yellow Sun Mk.2, so it gets identical dmg and aoe and a different range - the delivery changed, the warhead did not. ASMP is raised from 10.4 to 11.0 because the old justification was arithmetically wrong: entities.js:2150 holds a missile shot at range*0.88, so 10.4 fired from 9.15 tiles, INSIDE the 10.6 sam_area1 it claimed to stand outside. Both anchor lines (the yj6_c601 tail and the closing brace of W) are repeated so neither is dropped - the exact failure that produced a double comma in a previous run. Anchor verified count 1.

Two shared shapes beside the existing buff()/badger()/herc(), so each row below states only what differs - this file's established pattern. The Mirage comment drops the salvage design's false claim that it was 'faster than most fighters of its own decade': measured against the roster every e60 fighter is faster (Mirage IIIE 7.8 at js/eras.js:10370, against its 7.6). A second mount would not supplement Black Buck, it would REPLACE it: one pool of 6 against ammo 6 allows exactly one weapon a sortie, and pickWeapon scores a megaton round above twenty-one iron bombs at every range, so the aeroplane would never drop the load it is named for. (fireOtherMounts is not the reason — entities.js:1346 gates it on cat === "naval" and it never runs for an aircraft.)" Also strike "through fireOtherMounts" from measurement request 4.

fatals.problem: A CAPABILITY UNDERSTATED FOR A NATION THAT HAD IT, with a false historical justification written into the file. bluesteel range 9.6 means the Vulcan launches at 9.6 x 0.88 = 8.45 tiles, INSIDE the 10.6-tile sam_area1 of its own decade (rules.js:62; fielded by nato_e60_sam, pact_e60_sam, pla_e60_sam). The comment then defends this with "the RAF thought so too, which is why it wanted Skybolt's thousand miles". That is not what happened. In 1963 Blue Steel's ~185 km launch outranged every Soviet SAM by roughly four to one (SA-2 ~45 km); Skybolt was wanted for the 1970s threat and the coming low-level regime, not because the SA-2 could reach the launch point. Launching from outside the missile belt is the ONLY thing Blue Steel bought, and the plan's own card says so ("the only decade in which it could strike without flying over the target") while the number takes it away. The scale argument in the comment is also self-refuting: 8.6 tiles for the C-601's 100 km does not put 185 km "between" 8.6 and 11.0 — it puts it near 16.
fatals.correction: Either (a) raise `range: 9.6` to `range: 12.2` so the launch point is 10.74 tiles, just clear of sam_area1's 10.6, and raise `asmp` from 11.0 to 14.4 so the 1986 weapon is not out-ranged by the 1963 one (14.4 x 0.88 = 12.67, just clear of sam_area2's 12.5) — which also repairs the plan's own ASMP thesis; or (b) keep 9.6 and rewrite the justification honestly: "9.6 is a deliberate compression of the file's scale, not a claim that the SA-2 outranged Blue Steel — in 1963 it did not, by about four to one. What the number buys is that the Vulcan is under fire for two tiles of approach instead of flying the whole way in." Do NOT leave the current text, which asserts a reason the RAF did not have.

fatals.problem: "the American Skybolt on 22 December 1962 at Nassau". The Nassau conference ran 18–21 December 1962 and is where the POLARIS SUBSTITUTE was agreed; the Skybolt cancellation was a US decision conveyed to Thorneycroft on 11 December and confirmed around 22 December — it was not made at Nassau. The edit conflates the cancellation with the conference that answered it.
fatals.correction: "...and the American Skybolt in December 1962 — and it is the Skybolt cancellation that made Blue Steel the deterrent by default and sent Macmillan to Nassau on 18 December for the Polaris substitute agreed there on the 21st."

fatals.problem: REPEATS, IN SOFTENED FORM, THE DEFECT THE PLAN RAISES AGAINST THE SALVAGE DESIGN (its own finding 9). The header says the strike role "passed to the two-seat Mirage 2000N and later the Rafale B, which are fighter airframes carrying one missile and are on the French roster as fighters and strike aircraft". There is no Mirage 2000N row anywhere in UNITS — fra_e90_cas (js/eras.js:10465) is the CONVENTIONAL Mirage 2000D and bomber_f (js/rules.js:2234) is the Mirage 2000D RMV in role cas. No ASMP-armed French fighter exists in the tree. The sentence also mis-dates the handover: the Mirage 2000N took the ASMP role in 1988, eight years BEFORE the Mirage IVP left it, so the role did not "pass" in 1996 — it was shared from 1988 and ended on the IVP in 1996.
fatals.correction: "e00 and e20 EMPTY: the Mirage IVP flew its last nuclear alert on 1 July 1996. The ASMP role had already been shared since 1988 with the two-seat Mirage 2000N, and later with the Rafale B. Neither is on this roster as a nuclear aircraft — fra_e90_cas is the CONVENTIONAL Mirage 2000D and the Rafale is here as a fighter — and that is deliberate: a two-seat fighter carrying one missile is a fighter. The last Mirage IVs flew strategic RECONNAISSANCE, not strike, until 23 June 2005."

fatals.problem: "In 1962 the fleet was taken off high-level strike and handed to SACEUR for LOW level" compresses two events two years apart into one. The Valiant force was assigned to SACEUR in January 1960 in the tactical role; the switch from high level to low level came in 1962–63, after the U-2 shoot-down.
fatals.correction: "Assigned to SACEUR in 1960, and in 1962 taken off high-level strike and sent down LOW, because surface-to-air missiles had made 50,000 feet untenable — and low-level flying is what fatigued the rear spar."

fatals.problem: The mirage4() comment's own comparative figures do not match the numbers in the same edit. It says the Mirage IV "is a quarter of the radar target, and has a third of the reach" against a Buff. Measured against buff() and the B-52 rows: rcs 2.2 against 6.5 is a THIRD, and radius 46 against nato_e50_heavybomber's 96 is about HALF. (The "turns twice as well" claim is right: 1.3 against 0.55.)
fatals.correction: "...so it turns twice as well as a Buff, is a third of the radar target, and has half the reach."

fatals.problem: "launched at about 185 km at Mach 2.3 from 70,000 ft". 70,000 ft was Blue Steel's own cruise apogee after its post-release climb, not the Vulcan's release altitude — the high-level profile released at roughly 40,000–50,000 ft. Small, but it is the kind of number this file is audited on.
fatals.correction: "...launched at about 185 km from roughly 45,000 ft, climbing to 70,000 ft and cruising at Mach 2.3."

fatals.problem: MEASUREMENT REQUEST 3 predicts the wrong figure and would read as a failure when the tree is correct. It says fra_e80_heavybomber's sight should self-grow to "about 10.7". With asmp range 11.0 the sight loop (generations.js, INDIRECT_ROLE pass) gives round((11.0+0.4)*10)/10 = 11.4, and the later optics pass for fra at e80 (optics 0.94, bite 0.35 -> 0.979) gives 11.4 * (0.55 + 0.45*0.979) = 11.29 -> 11.3.
fatals.correction: Expect sight 11.3, not 10.7. (bluesteel likewise gives gbr_e60_heavybomber sight 10.0, not 9.)

fatals.problem: The Vulcan's second mount is effectively unreachable in play, and the comment claims otherwise. With ammo 6 on BOTH weapons against a pool floored to exactly 6, the first Blue Steel shot empties the pool, and entities.js:2160 then calls afterAttack() which returns {type:"rtb"} on ammo <= 0.05 — the aircraft goes home. Yellow Sun can only ever fire if the ordered target starts inside Blue Steel's 2.5-tile minRange. The comment's "pickWeapon reaches for ... the bomb only when the target is right underneath" is true of pickWeapon in isolation but not of any sortie the game will actually fly.
fatals.correction: Say what happens: "...and in practice that one weapon is Blue Steel, because the aeroplane launches at 8.4 tiles and turns for home with an empty pool. Yellow Sun is what it carries when the target is already inside the missile's 2.5-tile arming distance — which is the real 1963 choice, not a fallback." Or drop yellowsun2 from the mount list and keep it as a documented alternative fit.

reviews.reasoning:
Applicability: 13 of 14 anchors count exactly 1 in the live tree and every one is a complete syntactic unit - a whole line, a whole balanced {...} object (edit 9), a whole comment paragraph (edits 0, 5, 6, 7, 8), or a two-line pair whose halves are both reproduced at head and foot of the replacement (edits 1, 2, 3, 4). Edit 12 counts ZERO: js/ui.js:1080 stores the dash as the two-character escape — inside the string literal, and the plan's anchor carries a literal em dash. grep -c 'u2014' js/ui.js = 16 escape-form lines against 19 literal-em-dash lines elsewhere in the same file, so the file genuinely mixes the two and only the escape form matches this line.

I applied all 14 to copies of the LIVE files (the design agent's own scratch tree is not the live tree - its rules.js is 4352 lines against the live 4350, and its eras.js line citations run 50 low, so its 'applied cleanly to scratch copies' was not a test of what will actually be patched). The gbr_e60_tanker replacement re-parses with json.loads (32 keys) and matches the file's JSON-style quoting; the heavyair.js and air_specs.js rows match their files' JS style. No key collides: bluedanube, yellowsun2, bluesteel, blackbuck, an11_22, asmp, the five unit ids and the five AIRFRAMES ids each appear 0 times across js/. AIRFRAMES 131 -> 136, and every token used (planform delta, intake wingroot/cheek, fuselage heavy/area, tail ttail/single, htail none, camo silver/white/green/seagrey) already exists in that file.

Mechanism claims all held: manual is the flag (entities.js:503) and order.nuke is raised NOWHERE in the tree, so nuke:true really would be unreleasable; setOrder stamps release at entities.js:244; generations.js POOL floors heavybomber at 6 and only ever raises; dmul never scales range for a heavybomber (only acc via the guided term), so ASMP stays 11.0 and the 0.88 hold at entities.js:2152 launches at 9.68 tiles, outside sam_area1's 10.6 and inside sam_area2's 12.5 as claimed; privateWeapon copies every key so manual survives cloning; pickAirTarget does fall into the harvester branch for role heavybomber and the sweep branch's allWeaponsHeld guard exists at ai.js:4309; warAim returns {raid, ref} and buildings carry kind:'building' (entities.js:2769); every existing sead/ewair weapon carries antiRadiation:true, so edit 13 is bit-for-bit a no-op for the Weasel; no existing heavybomber carries a manual weapon and heavybomber is not in HELD_ROLES, so edit 11 is a no-op for the B-52 and H-6. The tanker hand-back bug is real: entities.js:2006 omits release and all four hand-backs (2253, 2266, 2282, 2296) assign straight to this.order. History checks out too (Blue Steel Feb 1963 on 617/27/83 and 100/139; Skybolt 22 Dec 1962; Valiant grounded 26 Jan 1965; Short Granite over Malden Island 15 May 1957; Mirage IV strike role ended 1 July 1996).

One permanent comment is factually wrong about the engine: edit 3 says a second held mount 'would be fired as a free extra by fireOtherMounts under any released attack order'. fireOtherMounts is called from exactly one site, entities.js:1346, gated on this.cat === 'naval'. No aircraft ever calls it. The conclusion (no WE.177B mount) still stands on the shared 6-unit pool and pickWeapon, but the stated reason is false and would be baked into the file. Not file-breaking, so SOUND_WITH_FIXES rather than BROKEN: nothing here corrupts a file, and the one unapplicable edit fails loudly at the anchor check rather than silently.
